d.title: Weight sharing across time is what makes it recurrent
d.caption: There is **one** weight matrix, applied at every timestep — not one per position. That is why an RNN handles a sequence of any length with a fixed parameter count, and also why its gradient is a product of T identical factors, which is the whole of 3.2's problem.

nodes.label: Gradient is W to the power T

d.title: The bottleneck: one vector has to carry the whole sequence
d.caption: Whatever the input's length, the final hidden state is a fixed-size vector — so a fifty-word sentence and a five-word one are both compressed into the same number of dimensions. Everything the decoder knows comes through that one vector, which is precisely the constraint attention (3.8) removes.

nodes.label: Read one step at a time

d.title: Measured: at a hundred steps the gradient is exactly zero
d.caption: Not small — **zero**. It underflowed float32 entirely, so the first hundred timesteps receive no gradient at all and the network is structurally unable to learn anything about them. And the column that explains why nobody notices: the gradient at the **last** step stays near 0.52 whatever the length, so the loss falls and the training curve looks healthy while the model has simply not read the beginning of its input. This measurement is where 'RNNs handle about 10–20 steps' comes from.

d.title: Why the decay is one-sided
d.caption: The gradient through T steps is a product of T factors, and a product's behaviour is asymmetric: anything below one shrinks **geometrically** toward zero, while anything above one grows geometrically toward overflow. The first failure is silent — small numbers just become smaller — and the second is loud, producing a NaN that stops the run. That is why vanishing is the harder problem: nothing tells you it happened.

nodes.label: So clipping solves one
nodes.sub: and gates are needed for the other

d.title: Clipping fixes the explosion and cannot touch the vanishing
d.caption: Clipping rescales the gradient when its norm exceeds a threshold, which preserves the **direction** and bounds the step. That stops a NaN dead. It does nothing whatsoever for a vanished gradient, because scaling zero up still gives zero — which is why clipping is a universally recommended safety measure and never the answer to a long-dependency problem.

d.title: Truncated BPTT, and the dependency it gives up
d.caption: Backpropagating through a ten-thousand-step sequence is impossible in memory, so the gradient is cut after k steps while the hidden state is **carried forward**. The consequence is precise: the model can still represent a dependency longer than k, because the state crosses the boundary, but it can never learn one — no gradient ever connects the two ends.

nodes.label: Memory is now O(k)
nodes.sub: which is why it is used anyway

d.title: A task with a dial on it
d.caption: The copy task exists to make memory length the **only** variable. The model sees a token, then T steps of noise, then must reproduce the token — so the required dependency is exactly T, set by you, and any failure is a memory failure rather than a modelling one. That is what makes it the right instrument for measuring where an architecture's ceiling actually is.

nodes.label: Only memory is tested
nodes.sub: no features, no pattern to find

nodes.label: So a failure is a memory failure
Turn the dial, find the ceiling

d.title: The gradient each position receives, RNN against LSTM
d.caption: At sixty steps the LSTM delivers 1.7e−12 to the first position where the RNN delivers 1.8e−17 — **five orders of magnitude more**. Both are tiny in absolute terms, and that is the honest reading: gating shifts the practical ceiling from around twenty steps to around a hundred, and does not remove it. Removing it is what attention does.

d.title: The result that did not fit, and the honest response to it
d.caption: The LSTM sat at **chance** from T = 20 while the vanilla RNN was perfect to T = 30 — the opposite of what the theory predicts. The right first response is that the setup is wrong rather than that LSTMs do not work, and the gradient measurements above rule out the obvious explanation: the LSTM's gradient at step 0 is *larger* at every length. So the architecture delivers what it promises and something else prevents the model using it — which §04 identifies as one line of initialisation.

d.title: One line of initialisation
d.caption: PyTorch initialises every LSTM bias near zero, so the forget gate starts at σ(0) = 0.5 — the cell state is **halved at every timestep** before training has learned otherwise, which is a decay of 0.5 to the power T and destroys exactly the long memory the architecture exists to provide. Setting that bias to 1 or 2 starts the gate open, and the task becomes learnable.

nodes.label: Long memory destroyed
nodes.sub: by the initialisation, not the design

d.title: The six equations, grouped by what they are for
d.caption: Three gates, a candidate, and two state updates. The grouping is the point: the three gates are each a sigmoid producing a number in (0, 1) that **multiplies** something, and the cell update is the only line that is additive — which is where the gradient highway of §03 comes from.

nodes.label: Forget gate f
nodes.sub: sigmoid: how much of c to keep

nodes.label: Input gate i
nodes.sub: sigmoid: how much new to admit

nodes.label: Candidate g
nodes.sub: tanh: what the new content is

nodes.label: Output gate o
nodes.sub: sigmoid: how much of c to expose

d.title: The gradient highway, and why it is the forget gate
d.caption: Differentiating cₜ = f⊙cₜ₋₁ + i⊙g gives ∂cₜ/∂cₜ₋₁ = **f** — so the gradient through the cell is a product of forget gates rather than a product of weight matrices. If f stays near 1 that product stays near 1 and the gradient survives hundreds of steps; if f is 0.5 it decays as 0.5ᵀ, which is exactly the failure 3.3 measured. The architecture gives you the highway; the initialisation decides whether it is open.

nodes.label: Gradient = product of f's
nodes.sub: not a product of weight matrices

d.title: What the forget-gate bias does before training starts
d.caption: The gate's initial value is σ(bias), and the cell's retention over T steps is that value to the power T. Read the last column: at the default bias of 0, **three per cent** of the signal survives 5 steps and nothing survives 50. At a bias of 2 the gate opens to 0.88 and 53% of the signal still survives 5 steps. This is the one-line change of 3.3, with its arithmetic.

d.title: The cost: exactly four times a vanilla RNN
d.caption: Four gates means four sets of weights, so the ratio is **exactly 4.00** at every size — not approximately. The textbook formula 4h(h+d) gives 364,544 for the first row against PyTorch's 366,592; the 2,048 difference is the two separate bias vectors PyTorch keeps for cuDNN compatibility, which are mathematically redundant with one another.

d.title: Four equations instead of six
d.caption: The GRU reaches the same goal with two gates rather than three, and — the structural difference — **no separate cell state**. One vector carries everything, which is why it has fewer parameters and why its gating is slightly less expressive: it cannot hold something in memory while hiding it from the next layer, because there is no hidden cell to hide it in.

columns.title: LSTM: six equations
items: h = o * tanh(c): exposure is gated

columns.title: GRU: four equations
items: h is the state: nothing to hide

d.title: The same gradient trick, in a different shape
d.caption: The GRU's update is h = (1−z)⊙hₜ₋₁ + z⊙h̃, which is a **convex combination** rather than the LSTM's independent keep-and-add. Differentiating gives (1−z), so the highway is still there and still gated — but the single z means admitting new content necessarily displaces old content in the same proportion, where the LSTM can do both independently.

nodes.label: LSTM uses f and i separately

d.title: Twenty-five per cent fewer parameters, and slower anyway
d.caption: The parameter ratio is exactly 0.750 at every size — arithmetic, not approximation. But on this CPU with torch 2.10 the GRU is **slower than the LSTM** at all three shapes, by 2.0×, 3.1× and 1.6×, because PyTorch's LSTM has a well-optimised fused CPU kernel and the GRU does not. The claim 'GRUs train faster' is correct about arithmetic and wrong about wall-clock here. Parameter and FLOP counts are a poor predictor of latency — the same lesson as the depthwise convolutions of 2.4.

d.title: Choosing between them
d.caption: The honest summary is that the choice rarely decides a project. Benchmark both on your own hardware if speed is the reason — §04 shows why the received wisdom is unreliable — and if long memory is the reason, set the LSTM's forget bias before concluding anything (3.3).

and spend the time on the data instead

d.title: The cost of bidirectionality is causality
d.caption: A bidirectional layer reads the sequence forwards and backwards and concatenates both states, so every position sees the **whole** sequence — which is why it helps so much on classification and tagging. It is unusable for anything that must run as the data arrives, because the backward pass cannot start until the sequence ends: no streaming, no generation, no real-time.

nodes.label: The backward pass needs the end
So: no streaming, no generation
nodes.sub: and no real-time use at all

d.title: Indexing the final state, which is where the bugs are
d.caption: Three traps in one line of code. With a **packed** batch the last valid step differs per sequence, so `output[:, -1]` reads padding for every sequence but the longest. With a **bidirectional** layer the forward and backward final states are at different ends. And `h_n` is shaped (layers × directions, batch, hidden), so taking `h_n[-1]` gives the last **direction** of the last layer rather than the concatenation.

nodes.label: With padding: wrong
nodes.sub: reads pad for all but the longest

nodes.label: h_n is (L x D, B, H)

d.title: Stacking, and what the second layer actually receives
d.caption: A stacked RNN feeds the **full sequence of hidden states** from layer one into layer two, not just the final state — so the second layer is reading a sequence of representations rather than a summary. Depth here buys abstraction in the same way it does in a CNN, and it is the reason two layers is usually a real improvement over one while five rarely is.

nodes.label: Layer 1
nodes.sub: outputs T x h, not just h_T

d.title: Dropout in the right place
d.caption: Standard dropout applied **across time** samples a different mask at every timestep, which injects fresh noise into the recurrence and prevents the state carrying information — it damages exactly what the RNN is for. Variational dropout fixes it by using the same mask at every step of a sequence. PyTorch's `dropout=` argument sidesteps the question by only dropping **between** layers, never within the recurrence.

nodes.label: Variational dropout
nodes.sub: the same mask all along the sequence

nodes.label: Safe, and limited
nodes.sub: does nothing for a single layer

d.title: The bottleneck, measured by what it has to fit
d.caption: The encoder's final state is a fixed vector — say 512 floats — and it must hold everything the decoder will need about an input of any length. For a short sentence that is ample; for a fifty-word one it is a lossy summary, and the loss falls on the **earliest** tokens, because they were overwritten first. Attention (3.8) is the response, and it works by deleting the bottleneck rather than widening it.

nodes.label: Encoder
nodes.sub: reads it one step at a time

d.title: Scheduled sampling, and the exposure bias it treats
d.caption: Teacher forcing trains the decoder on **ground-truth** previous tokens, but at inference it must consume its own predictions — so a single early mistake puts the model in a state it never saw in training, and errors compound. Scheduled sampling anneals from ground truth toward the model's own output during training, which narrows the gap and makes the training objective slightly inconsistent in exchange.

nodes.label: One early error compounds
nodes.sub: into states never seen in training

nodes.label: Anneal toward self-predictions
nodes.sub: a probability that rises per epoch

nodes.label: The gap narrows
nodes.sub: train and test look more alike

nodes.label: At a cost
nodes.sub: the objective is no longer exact

d.title: Attention in three steps, and what each one is
d.caption: Score every encoder state against the decoder's current state, normalise those scores to weights that sum to one, and take the **weighted average** of the encoder states. That is all of it. The output is a vector built freshly for every decoding step, which is why the fixed bottleneck disappears: nothing has to be summarised in advance.

d.title: Bahdanau and Luong: additive against multiplicative
d.caption: Two scoring functions with the same job. Bahdanau's concatenates the query and key and passes them through a small network with its own learned weights; Luong's takes a dot product, optionally through one matrix. The dot product has no parameters and maps onto a matrix multiply, which is why it is the one that scaled — the transformer's attention is Luong's, scaled.

columns.title: Bahdanau (additive)
items: Does not reduce to a matmul

columns.title: Luong (multiplicative)
items: score = q' k, or q' W k
No parameters in the dot form
Cheaper, and batches as one matmul

d.title: Why divide by the square root of d_k
d.caption: A dot product of two random d-dimensional vectors with unit-variance components has variance **d** — so as d grows the scores spread out, the softmax saturates, and its gradient goes to zero. Dividing by √d_k restores unit variance, which keeps the softmax in its responsive range. At d = 512 the unscaled standard deviation is 22.6, which is more than enough to make the softmax effectively a hard maximum.

d.title: Self-attention has no idea what order the tokens were in
d.caption: Attention is a weighted average over a **set**: permute the inputs and the outputs permute identically, with no other change. That is a genuine problem for language, where word order is meaning, and it is why position has to be injected explicitly rather than inferred — a sinusoidal encoding, a learned embedding, or a rotation applied inside the attention itself.

nodes.label: No notion of order at all

d.title: Multi-head attention, and why it is not just a wider one
d.caption: A single attention head produces one weighted average, so it can attend to one thing per position. Splitting d into h heads lets the layer attend to several relationships **at once** — syntax in one head, coreference in another — and costs nothing extra, because each head works in d/h dimensions and the total arithmetic is unchanged.

nodes.label: Same total arithmetic
nodes.sub: the width is divided, not added

d.title: Why greedy decoding is not the most likely sequence
d.caption: Greedy takes the highest-probability **token** at every step, which is not the same as the highest-probability **sequence** — a slightly worse first token can open a far better continuation, and greedy has already thrown it away. The search is over an exponentially large space and greedy explores exactly one path through it.

d.title: The length bias, and the normalisation that corrects it
d.caption: A sequence's score is a **sum of log probabilities**, and every token adds a negative number — so a longer sequence scores worse automatically, whatever its quality. Beam search therefore prefers short outputs, sometimes absurdly so. Dividing by the length removes the bias; dividing by length to a power α lets you tune how much, and α ≈ 0.6 to 0.7 is the usual setting in translation.

d.title: When not to use beam search
d.caption: Beam search optimises likelihood, and likelihood is the wrong objective whenever **diversity** is the point — which is why open-ended generation uses sampling instead. The failure is characteristic and well documented: large beams on open-ended text produce bland, repetitive output, because the most likely continuation of almost anything is a cliche.

d.title: Collapsing, and what the blank is for
d.caption: CTC's output is collapsed by removing repeats and then removing blanks — which creates an ambiguity the blank exists to resolve. Without it, 'hello' could never be produced, because the two l's would collapse into one; a blank placed between them keeps them separate. So the blank is not 'silence', it is a **separator**.

nodes.label: One label per input frame
nodes.sub: h h e - l l - l l o

d.title: Marginalising over alignments, without enumerating them
d.caption: The number of frame-level paths that collapse to a given transcript is exponential in the number of frames, so summing over them directly is impossible. CTC's loss is that sum computed by **dynamic programming** — the forward-backward algorithm — in time linear in frames and labels. That is the whole contribution: it makes an exponential sum tractable, which is why no alignment is needed.

nodes.label: The loss is their total probability

d.title: Running it, and the four arguments that go wrong
d.caption: Every one of these is a shape or convention detail rather than a concept, and every one produces a loss that trains to nonsense rather than an error. `log_probs` must be log-softmaxed, must be **time-first**, the blank index must match what the model was trained with, and both length tensors must be the true lengths rather than the padded ones.

d.title: Where CTC fits, and where it does not
d.caption: CTC assumes outputs are **monotonic** in the input and conditionally independent given the encoder — so it fits speech and handwriting, where the transcript follows the signal in order, and it does not fit translation, where words reorder. The independence assumption is also why a CTC model benefits so much from an external language model at decode time.

d.title: Packing is how the padding stops costing anything
d.caption: A packed sequence stores only the real timesteps plus the batch size at each step, so cuDNN simply stops computing a sequence once it ends — no wasted arithmetic and, crucially, **no spurious state updates**. The ordering requirement is the catch: pack wants the batch sorted by descending length unless `enforce_sorted=False`, and the returned `h_n` is already the correct final state per sequence, which is what makes it worth the ceremony.

d.title: Masking attention: where the mask has to be applied
d.caption: The mask must be applied to the **scores, before the softmax**, by setting padded positions to −∞. Zeroing the weights afterwards does not work: softmax has already given the padding a positive share, so zeroing leaves the remaining weights summing to less than one and silently scales the context vector down. Two different masks are needed and are often confused — padding masks what does not exist, causal masks what has not happened yet.

nodes.label: exp(-inf) = 0
nodes.sub: and the rest still sum to 1

nodes.label: Zeroing after softmax
nodes.sub: the weights no longer sum to 1

d.title: Masking the loss, and the reduction that quietly undoes it
d.caption: Even with a correct mask, `reduction='mean'` divides by the number of **elements** rather than the number of real tokens — so a batch that is one-third padding has its loss diluted by a third, and the dilution changes from batch to batch depending on composition. Use `ignore_index`, or sum and divide by the real token count yourself.

d.title: The RNN forward pass from scratch, as a loop over time
d.caption: One matrix per input, one per state, one bias — and a Python loop over timesteps. Writing it makes two things concrete that the module hides: the hidden state must be **initialised** before the loop, and every timestep's output has to be kept if the loss uses more than the final one.

d.title: BPTT: the gradient accumulates across time, it does not reset
d.caption: Because the same W is used at every timestep, its gradient is the **sum** of contributions from all T steps — which is the detail people get wrong when writing it by hand. And the gradient flowing into step t−1 is the gradient from step t multiplied by W, which is precisely the repeated multiplication that 3.2 measured decaying to zero.

nodes.label: dL/dW accumulates
nodes.sub: a sum over all T steps

d.title: Writing the LSTM cell: one matrix multiply, then a split
d.caption: The efficient implementation does not compute four gates separately — it concatenates the four weight matrices into one, does a **single** matrix multiply, and slices the result into four chunks before applying the activations. That is why the weight tensors in PyTorch's LSTM have a leading dimension of 4h, and why the gate order in that tensor is a convention you must match when loading weights by hand.

nodes.label: Split into four chunks
nodes.sub: i, f, g, o - in that order

d.title: What the two cells deliver, measured at the first position
d.caption: The same measurement as 3.3, from the hand-written cells. The LSTM delivers more gradient to step 0 at **every** length, and the ratio widens with depth in time: 2.7× at ten steps, 254× at thirty, and about a hundred thousand times at sixty. Both are still tiny at sixty, which is the honest conclusion — gating moves the ceiling, attention removes it.

d.title: An embedding is a lookup table that happens to be a matrix multiply
d.caption: One-hot encoding a vocabulary of 50,000 and multiplying by a weight matrix selects **one row** of that matrix — so the multiplication is pure waste, and an embedding layer is the same operation implemented as an indexed read. That equivalence is why an embedding's gradient is sparse: only the rows for tokens actually present in the batch receive one.

nodes.label: Almost all of it is waste

d.title: The analogy, geometrically, and what it does not prove
d.caption: king − man + woman landing near queen means the **difference vector** between those pairs is roughly shared, which is a real and useful property of the space. It is also routinely over-claimed: the nearest neighbour is often one of the three input words and must be excluded, the result depends on the normalisation, and the analogies that work are the ones the corpus made frequent.

d.title: Where embeddings come from
d.caption: The division that matters is **static against contextual**. Word2Vec and GloVe give one vector per word for all time, so 'bank' has a single compromise representation; a transformer gives a different vector per occurrence, which is why contextual embeddings replaced static ones for almost everything except where a fixed lookup table is itself the requirement.
